141: Accurate specimen labeling ensures the right sample reaches the lab and is matched to the correct patient, preventing misidentification errors that cause rejected specimens, repeat draws, and delayed results. While billing and HIPAA are related to healthcare operations, the primary laboratory concern is patient safety and timely, correct testing.
142: Voice mail systems accept messages when staff are unavailable, so callers can leave information instead of encountering a busy signal. Unlike live reception, voicemail does not guarantee immediate human contact or call routing.
143: Patient identification must exactly match the requisition to prevent wrong-patient errors—a leading cause of specimen mix-ups. Any discrepancy requires stopping the draw and resolving the mismatch with nursing or the ordering provider before proceeding.
144: A fax machine transmits document images over telephone lines to remote locations, enabling rapid sharing of requisitions, results, or orders outside the office. Pagers, photocopiers, and word processors do not perform this remote document transmission function.
145: Thermal fax paper uses heat-sensitive coating that darkens when exposed to heat from the print head, producing the image. This material can fade over time and is not permanent, which is why important faxed records are often copied onto standard paper.
146: Expiration dates indicate the last day a product may be used; tubes dated 12.05.2011 remain acceptable through that entire date. Using tubes beyond expiration risks loss of vacuum, additive degradation, and unreliable test results.
147: Collection date and time are mandatory label elements because many analytes change with time, and timing affects interpretation of timed tests and medication levels. Barcodes and accession numbers support tracking but are not universally required on every label, and tube fill volume is not a standard label field.
148: Requisitions specify the ordering physician, tests ordered, and collection timing—not the exact blood volume, which the phlebotomist determines from tube requirements and test needs. Volume is dictated by tube type and laboratory protocols rather than the order form.
149: Universal Serial Bus (USB) refers to external storage devices such as flash drives that hold data outside the computer's CPU. Software runs programs, middleware connects systems, and a LIS is an application—not hardware for external data storage.
150: Standard patient identification requires at least two unique identifiers (such as full name, date of birth, and medical record number) before any specimen collection. This dual-identifier practice is a Joint Commission and CLSI requirement to prevent wrong-patient events.
151: Gloves provide barrier protection against a broad range of bloodborne pathogens including bacteria and viruses, not viruses alone. They protect both the healthcare worker and the patient by reducing bi-directional transmission of microorganisms.
152: Material Safety Data Sheets (MSDS/SDS) document chemical hazards, exposure limits, and required PPE—not commercial pricing. Manufacturers must provide safety information; cost data is a purchasing concern, not a safety document element.
153: The Joint Commission is a voluntary, nongovernmental accrediting body that sets hospital operational and quality standards. CAP focuses on laboratory accreditation, CMS handles Medicare/Medicaid, and ASCLS is a professional society—not a hospital accreditor.
154: CLSI (formerly NCCLS) publishes evidence-based standards for specimen collection, handling, and processing that guide phlebotomy practice. CAP accredits labs, CDC provides public health guidance, and OSHA regulates workplace safety—not phlebotomy technique standards specifically.
155: Direct contact transmission occurs when an infectious agent passes from an infected person to a susceptible host through physical touch, such as blood or body fluid contact. Fomite and vehicle transmission involve contaminated objects or substances as intermediaries.
156: Gloves must be changed between every patient to prevent cross-contamination and nosocomial infection spread. Waiting until gloves are visibly soiled or only changing for known infectious patients leaves patients and staff at unnecessary risk.
157: OSHA's Hazard Communication Standard requires Material Safety Data Sheets (now Safety Data Sheets) for all hazardous chemicals in the workplace. These documents detail chemical properties, health effects, and safe handling—not HIPAA privacy or NFPA fire codes alone.
158: Class C and ABC fire extinguishers are designed for energized electrical equipment because they use non-conductive extinguishing agents. Class A extinguishers address ordinary combustibles and Class B covers flammable liquids—neither is appropriate for live electrical fires.
159: OSHA-approved safety-engineered needles with built-in sharps injury protection significantly reduce needlestick injuries when used with proper technique. Recapping, uncapped disposal, and placing needles in biohazard bags (instead of sharps containers) increase exposure risk.
160: HIPAA (Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act) establishes federal standards for protecting patient health information privacy and security. The Affordable Care Act reformed insurance access; HIPAA specifically governs protected health information.
161: The greatest reduction in accidental bloodborne pathogen exposure comes from combining safer engineered devices with consistent safe work practices. Neither equipment alone nor containers alone provides complete protection without proper technique and compliance.
162: The MSDS/SDS is the authoritative workplace document for chemical hazard identification, exposure limits, and required safety precautions. Bottle labels give basic warnings but lack the comprehensive safety detail found on the MSDS.
163: Isolation precautions exist primarily to interrupt transmission of communicable diseases among patients, staff, and visitors. While they may involve PPE and education, the core purpose is infection prevention—not general hospital cleanliness.
164: OSHA regulates workplace safety including medical waste handling and disposal requirements for healthcare facilities. The CDC provides infection control guidance, CLIA governs lab testing quality, and the DEA regulates controlled substances—not general biohazard waste disposal.
165: Hand sanitizers are a protective measure, not a route of biohazard exposure. Common exposure routes include percutaneous (needlestick), ingestion (contaminated hands to mouth), mucous membrane contact, and airborne transmission of infectious particles.
166: Natural rubber latex in gloves, tourniquets, and some collection devices is a common allergen that can cause reactions ranging from contact dermatitis to anaphylaxis. Nitrile and vinyl are latex-free alternatives for sensitized patients and staff.
167: Syncope (fainting) results from vasovagal stimulation causing bradycardia and hypotension, which reduces cerebral blood flow. It is a common complication during phlebotomy, especially in anxious or fasting patients, and requires immediate safety measures.
168: Hepatitis B virus remains infectious in dried blood on surfaces for up to seven days, making environmental contamination a real concern. HIV does not survive long outside the body, HCV is bloodborne (not fecal), and CDC standard precautions require gloves during blood collection.
169: Patients with suspected or confirmed latex allergy must receive latex-free gloves, tourniquets, and collection supplies to prevent allergic reactions. Continuing to use latex despite patient concern violates standard safety practice and puts the patient at risk.
170: Forcing a blood draw on a resisting child without consent constitutes battery—the unlawful touching of a person. Restraint and forced procedure without appropriate consent or legal authority also raises assault concerns and violates patient rights.
171: Professional ethics encompasses competent compassionate care, functioning at the highest professional standard, and adhering to legal and regulatory requirements—all three together define ethical healthcare practice. Ethics is not merely about avoiding lawsuits but about comprehensive professional conduct.
172: Risk management is the systematic process of identifying, assessing, and minimizing situations that could cause patient harm, employee injury, or institutional loss. It proactively addresses potential problems before they result in adverse events or liability.
173: A Durable Power of Attorney for healthcare designates a trusted person to make medical decisions when the patient cannot communicate their wishes. A living will states treatment preferences but does not appoint a decision-maker; informed consent authorizes a specific procedure.
174: The four elements of malpractice are duty, dereliction (breach of duty), direct cause, and damages—often remembered as the four Ds. A code of ethics guides professional behavior but is not a legal element required to prove malpractice.
175: A tort is a civil wrong causing injury to a person or property, distinct from criminal acts. Assault and battery are specific types of torts involving threats or unwanted physical contact, but tort is the broader legal category.
176: Battery is the unlawful physical contact with a patient, such as performing a venipuncture without consent. Assault is the threat of harm; the actual unauthorized blood draw constitutes battery because it involves unwanted touching.
177: Direct cause (proximate cause) means the healthcare provider's action directly led to the patient's injury, as when improper cast application caused the leg to heal incorrectly. The injury must be a foreseeable result of the negligent act.
178: Documentation provides objective evidence of whether standard of care was met or deviated from, making it critical in malpractice cases. Without proper records, neither compliance nor negligence can be reliably established in court.
179: A subpoena is a legal court order compelling a specific person to appear and testify or produce evidence at a designated time. It is not a contract, agent agreement, or voluntary arrangement between parties.
180: Implied consent applies in life-threatening emergencies when the patient cannot communicate and immediate action is needed to preserve life—such as performing CPR on an unresponsive patient. Expressed consent requires verbal or written agreement for non-emergency procedures.
181: A law is a rule of conduct established and enforced by a governing authority with legal force. Principles and policies guide behavior but lack the enforceable authority of statutory or regulatory law.
182: Leukocytes (white blood cells) are the immune cells responsible for fighting infection and inflammation. Erythrocytes are red blood cells that carry oxygen; lymphocytes and monocytes are specific types of leukocytes.
183: The central nervous system consists of the brain and spinal cord, which integrate and process nerve signals. Peripheral nerves, dendrites, and axons are components of the peripheral nervous system, not the CNS itself.
184: The phlebotomist's primary role is obtaining blood specimens through venipuncture and capillary puncture for laboratory analysis. Medical assistants have broader clinical duties; cytologists and pathologists analyze specimens rather than routinely collect them.
185: Type O blood lacks both A and B antigens on the red cell surface, making it the universal donor for red cells in emergency situations. Types A and B each carry one antigen; type AB carries both.
186: The blood bank (immunohematology/transfusion service) performs ABO/Rh typing, antibody screening, and crossmatching required for safe transfusion. Hematology performs CBCs; chemistry and microbiology do not determine blood type for transfusion.
187: Histology is the microscopic study of tissues and cells for disease diagnosis. Cytology examines individual cells (often from fluids or smears); hematology studies blood; phlebotomy is the practice of blood collection.
188: Dehydration reduces plasma volume relative to cellular components, causing hemoconcentration—artificially elevated values for proteins, cells, and other analytes in the remaining smaller plasma volume. This is why proper hydration status matters when interpreting lab results.
189: Capillary puncture uses a lancet or puncture device to obtain small blood volumes from the finger or heel. Needles, syringes, and evacuated tube systems are used for venipuncture, not standard capillary collection.
190: The integumentary system comprises the skin, hair, nails, and associated glands—the body's outer protective barrier. Kidneys belong to the urinary system; muscles to the muscular system; bones to the skeletal system.
191: PSA (prostate-specific antigen) is a tumor marker screened from blood to assess prostate health in males. PAP is a cervical cytology test; RPR screens for syphilis; CAD refers to coronary artery disease.
192: Leukocytes are the body's primary defense against infection through phagocytosis, antibody production, and immune signaling. Erythrocytes transport oxygen; platelets participate in clotting; fibrinogen conversion is part of the coagulation cascade.
193: Standard Precautions are the first and foundational CDC tier, applied to all patients regardless of diagnosis to prevent healthcare-associated infections. Transmission-based isolation precautions (contact, droplet, airborne) are the second tier for known or suspected infections.
194: Formed elements are the cellular components of blood—erythrocytes, leukocytes, and platelets—suspended in plasma. Serum is plasma without clotting factors; whole blood includes both plasma and formed elements.
195: Sputum cultures detect respiratory pathogens such as bacteria causing pneumonia, tuberculosis, or bronchitis. The specimen comes from the lower respiratory tract, making it a respiratory system diagnostic test.
196: The prefix hyper- means excessive, above normal, or increased, as in hypertension (high blood pressure) or hyperglycemia (high blood glucose). Hypo- means below normal; eu- means normal.
197: The liver, stomach, mouth, and pancreas are organs of the digestive system responsible for ingestion, digestion, absorption, and processing of nutrients. They are not part of the reproductive, sensory, or muscular systems.
198: Blood cultures detect bacteremia or septicemia—bacteria or fungi circulating in the bloodstream, which can be life-threatening. They are not used to diagnose anemia, cholesterol levels, or cancer directly.
199: When no blood flows after venipuncture, the needle bevel may be against the vein wall or not fully within the lumen; gently repositioning or rotating the needle often restores flow. Immediately restarting or advancing the needle risks hematoma or through-and-through puncture.
200: Post-prandial means after eating; a 2-hour post-prandial glucose specimen is collected exactly two hours after the patient begins or finishes a meal, per the ordering protocol. This timing reflects how the body metabolizes glucose after food intake.
201: Diabetes mellitus is a chronic metabolic disorder characterized by insufficient insulin secretion or insulin resistance, leading to hyperglycemia. The pancreas produces insulin; its failure to secrete adequate amounts defines this condition.
202: The bleeding time test evaluates primary hemostasis—specifically platelet plug formation and capillary vasoconstriction at the wound site. It does not measure vessel pressure, elasticity, or venous blockage.
203: Pathology is the comprehensive study of disease processes in the body, including cause, mechanism, and structural/functional changes. Hematology focuses on blood disorders; histology on tissue structure; phlebotomy on specimen collection.
204: The pre-analytical phase encompasses everything before actual laboratory analysis: test ordering, patient preparation, specimen collection, labeling, transport, and processing. Errors in this phase are the most common source of laboratory mistakes.
205: Peak and trough levels measure the highest and lowest serum drug concentrations to assess therapeutic range and dosing for medications such as antibiotics, anticonvulsants, and digoxin. Timing relative to the last dose is critical for accurate interpretation.
206: Needle redirection may be necessary when the vein rolls due to inadequate anchoring, the patient moves unexpectedly, or blood flow starts then stops—each situation may require slight needle adjustment. All listed scenarios are valid indications for careful repositioning.
207: Complete specimen labeling requires the patient's name and unique identifier, date and time of collection, and the collector's initials to ensure traceability and correct result reporting. Omitting any element compromises specimen integrity and patient safety.
208: A hematoma is a localized collection of blood in subcutaneous tissue caused by leakage from a punctured vein during venipuncture. Petechiae are tiny pinpoint hemorrhages; hemolysis is red cell destruction within the tube.
209: Cholesterol testing requires serum from a red-top (no additive) or gold SST tube that allows clotting and yields serum after centrifugation. Additive tubes (lavender EDTA, blue citrate, yellow specialized) are used for other test categories.
210: The middle (third) and ring (fourth) fingers are preferred for adult capillary puncture because they are less sensitive than the index finger and less prone to infection than the little finger. The pulp of these fingers provides adequate blood flow with minimal patient discomfort.
